report:
### Conclusion
The claim is **partially true**, but its benefits depend heavily on environmental conditions and fire safety considerations. 

### Evidence Supporting the Claim
Research demonstrates that opening an internal door or window increases bedroom ventilation and lowers carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) levels. In sealed bedrooms, $\text{CO}_2$ produced by human respiration often exceeds 2,000 ppm. Studies indicate that keeping $\text{CO}_2$ below 1,000 ppm through open windows or doors increases deep sleep, improves sleep efficiency, and enhances next-day alertness (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/ina.12435, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132323011459).

### Counterevidence and Risks
* **Fire Safety:** The UL Fire Safety Research Institute (FSRI) strongly recommends sleeping with interior doors **closed**. A closed door acts as a barrier against heat, smoke, and flames during a home fire, providing critical extra time to escape (https://fsri.org/news/surprising-reason-you-should-leave-your-door-closed-when-you-sleep).
* **Noise and Air Quality:** Opening windows can admit ambient noise, pollen, outdoor air pollution, and extreme temperatures, which frequently disrupt sleep cycles and aggravate respiratory issues (https://molekule.com/blogs/all/sleep-window-open-night).

### Summary
While improved airflow from open doors or windows can boost sleep quality by preventing $\text{CO}_2$ buildup, it can compromise fire safety or introduce outdoor disturbances. Mechanical ventilation, air purifiers, or leaving windows slightly cracked while keeping interior doors shut often provide a safer middle ground.
